title: Heart Sutra Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Heart Sutra, starting with the story of Xuanzang, the seventh-century Chinese monk who snuck out of China after a dream and walked India for 16 years before bringing the sutra back. Nomon reads the longer preface that sets the scene, with Shariputra asking Avalokiteshvara how to practice prajnaparamita, and then goes through the five skandhas one at a time: form, sensations, perception, formations, and consciousness. The lectern becomes an image for emptiness, as oak, then wood, then cells and atoms that are mostly space. Nomon closes on things going sideways and later turning out to be exactly what needed to happen.

Anyway, the Heart Sutra.
The Heart Sutra is very central.
It's hard to underestimate how central it seems to be in Mahayana Buddhism, which says Zen is a part of Mahayana Buddhism.

It's recited daily, as we just did, at Zen centers and temples and monasteries all over the world in all kinds of languages: Chinese, Japanese, English, Spanish, French, German, who knows what languages.
In Japan, all of the Buddhist schools at some point, I don't know when they did this, early on, somehow all agreed on the same translation.
A similar thing happened in America about 10 years ago, 15 maybe.
So more or less everybody's, not all of them, but most everyone's doing the translation we're doing.
If you go to Japan or you go to any Japanese or Japan lineage center all around the world, they all chant the Heart Sutra in the exact same way.
They all ended up using the same translation, although they chant the Chinese characters with the Japanese voicing of them.
The translation that they use is the translation of a really amazing character.
In the seventh century, there was a pilgrim from China, a Chinese Buddhist monk named Zhuanzang, which is maybe more or less how he said his name, Zhuanzang.
Somehow he got inspired.
He had a dream.
We don't listen to our dreams enough.
He had a dream that he needed to go to India and study Buddhism at the source.
So he snuck out of the country.
You weren't supposed to leave the country.
China had many periods where they didn't want you to leave, a very closed, huge place, but it's still a closed society, closed borders.
So he snuck out and he walked around India for 16 years, just because of a dream.
When he was on his way back, having collected all kinds of sutras in his backpack, there are wonderful pictures of him with his big wicker backpack, which is full of scrolls.
He went all around India studying, went to the major monastic universities, went to many centers, and he took really good notes, he had a really good journal.
Among the things he brought back was the Heart Sutra, or in Sanskrit.
Then he did a translation, and it's Zhuanzang's translation that's the standard translation, chanted all over the Japanese Buddhist world.
So if you memorize that, which we do every once in a while on Saturday morning, even if you don't know a single word anyone else is saying, you'll hear, and you'll know what to do.
You'll fit right in.
I had that experience one time in Zurich, actually.
There's a Dharma talk in German, which I didn't understand a word of, but I got a chance with the Heart Sutra.
One interesting theory about the Heart Sutra is that there's a strange anomaly with this sutra.
Several things are strange about it.
One is it's very short.
Most sutras are much longer.
Another is that it's about wisdom.
It's about the Prajnaparamita, the wisdom beyond wisdom.
There's a whole huge set of sutras about this topic.
We studied one of them last fall, or two falls ago, I forget what it was, called the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 lines, and there are different lengths, much longer than that.
But the Heart Sutra, even though it purports to be a part of that literature, has a very different style.
Much of the word choice is different than found in all the other sutras.
And the oldest existing manuscript is Chinese.
The oldest Chinese translation is older than the oldest Sanskrit, supposedly original.
So one theory is that it might be Xuanzang made it up.
Maybe he wrote it and then later did a Sanskrit version.
You have to do that for legitimacy purposes.
Who knows?
There's one major scholar who says that, and not everyone agrees with her.
Probably the most likely is it was indeed written in the early period of the formation of that literature, which was 100 to about 350 in the common era.
The religious story, the religious point of view, is that the Heart Sutra, like all sutras, was spoken by the Buddha and written down by his disciples who memorized what he said.
But then they had to handle the problem that the teachings of the Heart Sutra are not in all the other early Buddhist teachings.
Elements are there.
It's still Buddhism.
But teachings in that style are not in the early writings.
So the way they handled that problem was to say that after the Buddha gave that talk, he realized that the monks and nuns weren't ready for it.
So one of his assistants gave it to the Nagas for safekeeping.
The Nagas are like underwater dragons.
They're serpents that live underwater in palaces, huge palaces, deep underwater.
So the Nagas held on to it for, whatever, 800 years until we were ready for it.
Now all Buddhist sutras, since they're spoken by the Buddha, usually start out explaining, setting the scene, telling you where you are and that the Buddha is speaking and who he's talking to.
But you may have noticed that our version of the Heart Sutra does not say that.
Does anyone have a chant book?
It would be helpful if we all had chant books.
We put them away, we're so tidy.
Is there one more in there?
Probably can all find that pretty easily.
Page four.
Ours does not start out with the Buddha.
It doesn't really explain who's there or where it's happening.
It starts out with Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, who is a kind of goddess or bodhisattva of compassion.
Well, it turns out there's a longer version that sets the scene.
I thought you'd like to know what's happening.
This longer version is more often recited and studied in Tibetan Buddhism.
The earliest manuscripts of that are yet a little older.
So maybe the longer version is, I mean a little newer, excuse me, a little newer.
So maybe this longer version was also written later to fill in this problem.
Who knows?
Here's the beginning of the longer version.
It's like the preface from our point of view.
*Thus have I heard it one time.
The Buddha was in Rajagriha on the mountain of Gurdrakuta,* which is Bolter Peak, *along with the great sangha of bhikkhus,* monks.
*And that time the Buddha entered into the great, vast, extremely profound samadhi.* So he went into deep meditation.
*And within the multitude of beings there, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva began practicing the profound prajnaparamita.
And when she illuminated the five skandhas, she saw they were all empty and left all suffering,* ended all suffering.

*And then Shariputra, by the power of the Buddha, joined his palms together in respect to the noble Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva, and said, virtuous one, if there are those who wish to cultivate the extremely profound practice of prajnaparamita, how should they cultivate that practice?*
So that's the preface.
The Buddha was there, but the Buddha is in deep meditation.
Avalokiteshvara is among the assembly and also in a deep practice, focused on wisdom, prajnaparamita.
Then Shariputra is one of the Buddha's 80 chief disciples.
He had 80 chief disciples.
They have all these numbers in Buddhism, so he had exactly 80 chief disciples.
Shariputra was known for his understanding of the early wisdom texts, and we met him in the other prajnaparamita sutra also.
Shariputra shows up in most of them.
In that case, he was with another monk, brain just turned off.
Subhuti, very good, Subhuti, exactly.
Subhuti had to explain a lot of stuff to him.
Now Avalokiteshvara is going to explain stuff to poor Shariputra.
Shariputra is like the brainiest guy in class.
He doesn't quite get it.
It's good that he's there because otherwise we wouldn't understand it either.
Exactly.
But then the interesting part of this preface is that Shariputra receives like a psychic instruction from the Buddha.

It said in there, *Shariputra, by the power of the Buddha, joined his palms together and asked this question.* So the Buddha is like behind the scenes directing this show, inspired Shariputra to ask this question.
So our whole sutra is Avalokiteshvara's answer.
We get a really condensed setting of the scene.
For us, the entire setting of the scene is the first sentence.
*That Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, when deeply practicing Prajnaparamita, clearly saw that all five aggregates are empty and thus relieved all suffering.*
Then if we were really nice, we would have quote marks before the word Shariputra, because that's now Avalokiteshvara speaking.
So he's saying, okay Shariputra, here's your answer.
But we omit the question, right?
So how would you know what's going on?
The first time, when I was in Mexico in December, one of the students there asked me, who is this Shariputra?
What's the secret here?
So the first sentence also overlaps a little bit in the introduction.

The introduction mentioned also that Avalokiteshvara was in this deep practice of Prajnaparamita, and something that she saw, something that she understood in this practice, about the five aggregates.
What I read here, did it say five skandhas?
What I read here first said five skandhas.
So when you think about these five somethings, understanding whatever this is clearly frees you from suffering.
So this must be pretty important.
Five aggregates in our text is an English translation of the Sanskrit word skandha.
I think the previous translation we had did say skandha, they changed it to aggregates.
Is that right John?
Maybe it would be better to stick with skandhas, but all translations have problems.
This is better in many other ways.
The aggregates or the skandhas are a reference to Buddhist psychology.
One of the early ways that the Buddha suggested that we re-understand our life and our experience is a practice called the five skandhas.
It's usually explained as a list, but really it's a practice.
All these things are process, all these things are active, things that we do.
We have to learn about them a little bit so we can do them, but we have to do them for them to have any useful life.
The idea is that we take in all kinds of stuff.
We're always perceiving things, we're always thinking things, we're always planning and remembering and worrying and moving and doing stuff in the world.
And we turn the sum of all that into some kind of a narrative, some kind of a story.

This is me going along, I'm this kind of person, I have these kind of problems, and maybe once in a blue moon I remember I have these kind of strengths, and here I am, this is me, me, me, me, me, me, me, me, me, until there's no more me, me, me.
The Buddha suggested that's not a very useful way to understand our reality, that it's a way that's very much prone to suffering, because it's all about me.
Can I get enough?
Can I protect myself?
I'm worried about me, my inadequacies, my sense of lack.
I'm worried they're going to actually notice me.
Please don't notice me, no matter what you do, or whatever it is.
Or everyone should notice me, depending on your condition.
The Buddha said look more carefully.
Look more carefully at every moment of experience.
Slow yourself down, so meditation is helpful, and see if you can catch it, like right as it appears.
What is this moment?
What is this moment?
What is this moment?

He suggested if you look really carefully, you'll see that everything that happens, so-called outside and so-called inside, and there's no distinction in Buddhist psychology between outside and inside, everything that happens actually is just a little moment of experience that fits into these five categories.
The original word skandha means heaps, like piles, like sorting things into piles.
Everything that happens is actually just something you could put in one of these five piles, in these five categories.
And if you understand this clearly, he said, and you really experience it, there won't be any more suffering.
So we should learn these categories and see if we can practice them and notice them.
I think this is another area where sometimes the English falls down a little, or any non-Buddhist language, so it might be useful to learn the Sanskrit.
The first category is rupa, which means form.
Form is pretty good, usually translated as form.
Form is just physicality, physical stuff: our body, the stuff we can see and touch and taste and so on.
In Western thought, this is reality.
Form is the whole of reality, because anything you can't see or measure doesn't really exist.
And in Western thought, there's a big difference between form and thought, or form and spirit.
Form and non-form is the big distinction.
But in Buddhist psychology, form is just one of several categories.
So we can notice when we're interacting with form and see if we can see it as form, just as form.
The second category is vedana, which is translated here as feelings.
No?
Translated as sensations.
Yeah, that's really bad.
Okay, well, translation.
So vedana.
Usually translated as feelings, in our sutra now translated as sensations.
This is feelings or sensations meant in a particular way.
This is my favorite Skandha.
It's the low and almost instantaneous way the mind seems to lean forward and back, left and right: pleasant, unpleasant.
Like it, don't like it.
There seems to be a very root duality [unclear: "into like an adverb"].
Dividing in half: this, that, this, that.
Like it, don't like it.
Pleasant, unpleasant.
And it seems to happen even before cognition, actually.
So the idea is that we can slow things down a little bit and see if we can start to separate these mental events.
When we notice pleasant and unpleasant, it's often associated with an object, right?
Oh, I like looking at Jeff.
I don't like looking at trash.
But the way it's understood, it's not really attached to that object.
It just somehow arose in some relationship to that object, and they're two different experiences.
So the idea is that you can eventually notice something like: hearing.
Now sound, hearing, hearing, unpleasant.
Which is a very different way of experiencing the world than some thought like, "I really hate that techno music.
Why do they play that?
It's too loud.
How can anyone like this?"
So the practice is to be able to just experience directly that little sense of like it, don't like it.
Pleasant, unpleasant.

And to see the way that winds us up and drives us around and leads to all kinds of thinking and perception that actually is designed to justify the reality and sensibleness of that original leaning, that original feeling.
"Of course I don't like that.
Who would like that?
Nobody would like that."
So that's the second Skandha, very important.
Meditation really helps us to see it a little bit differentiated, and not so caught in the object it's associated with and not so caught in the story that we build around it.
The third Skandha, samjhna, which is really hard to say, is perception.
This is pretty similar to the Western idea of perception.
There's a whole complicated other thing about it which we won't get into, but it's what comes in through the senses, really just at that point of perception.
So, for instance, light, color, not flower, or pitch, timber, volume, not fire truck.
Just the direct feeling of perception.
The one difference between Buddhist perception and Western perception is that in Buddhism there's a sixth sense.
The first five are the same.
Sense number six is that quality of mind that can see thoughts, that can perceive a thought arising.
So the mind is not just seen as what's thinking; the mind is seen as what is seeing the thinking, perceiving the thinking.
What is doing the thinking?
Nobody.
But that's a whole other story.
In Western thought you need a self to do the thinking.
Here we don't have that self so much.
So that's the third Skandha.
We had form, rupa; feelings, vedana; samjhna, perception.
The fourth category is a really big category.
This is where we hang out most of the time.
The fourth category is samskara, samskara.
The translation here is formations, which is pretty good.
Sometimes you see impulses, sometimes a few other words, but formations is the most common, which is good because it's probably the best.
This is the thought field, basically.
This is the way we take the existence of physicality, the leaning of the mind back and forth, the perceiving of things coming in, inside and outside, and we turn it into mental stuff.
Fabrications, that's another word they use, fabrications.
We basically think that's reality.
And again in this system it's just one of a variety of experiences that can happen to a human being.
It's more real than anything else.
It's the putting together of stuff.
The etymology of the word samskara is that which has been put together, that which isn't put together.
So our mind has put some stuff together to create something like racism or food co-op or career or banana or something like that.
Anything.
That's the fourth Skandha, and you'll see those as thoughts that we assemble.
Real in its way, right?
But also not real.
Also just an assembly of impulses and experiences.
The fifth and last of the five Skandhas is vijnana, vijnana, and that's consciousness.
That's pretty much like Western consciousness, a little different, but it's the quality of awareness, of just being aware.
If you imagine all this happening without the fifth Skandha, then we would have basically no self-awareness, right?
We might be really present in a certain way, but we wouldn't have the self-awareness to know what we were actually doing.
We would just be responding to everything.
You could probably live a pretty functional Western life and make a lot of money and do a good job, I don't know.
But you wouldn't have any awareness of what you were doing.
It's like in your mind, there are so many yous, right?
There's an observer and somebody who's stuck in the thoughts and all these different things.
And then there's this overall sense that, wow, there's all this stuff happening in here.
So that's consciousness.
It's not just the observer, actually.
Sometimes it's misunderstood as the observer.
That's just another samskara.
So early Buddhism said, you can just cut it out with this mi-mi-mi thing.
Perceive it directly as these five Skandhas, progressive, on the path, and be relieved from suffering.
And this is taking this a step further.
This is saying, well, that's true, and, and, it's a big and, that Avalokiteshvara saw that these five aggregates, these five Skandhas, are empty, are empty.
So the key word here is empty.
What are they empty of?
What does this mean?
This whole later Buddhist movement revolved around two primary ideas.
One is emptiness, and the other is the archetype of the Bodhisattva.
And I suppose Prajnaparamita is an offshoot of both of those, a certain kind of wisdom.
Avalokiteshvara goes on to try to explain for the rest of the sutra what she means by empty.
So we'll end with this next section.
The problem with the Heart Sutra is it's hard to get very far through this one-page text.
*She said, well, Shariputra, form does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from form.
Form itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself is form.
Form itself is empty.*
It seems like we're missing an "is" in there.
Anyway.
Emptiness is the sense that nothing really can stand up on its own.
Everything is more fluid, more changing, more dependent on other things than we can possibly imagine.
So it's beyond imagination and conceptualization.
There are all kinds of interesting intellectual roads towards emptiness and also practice roads towards emptiness.
Again, it's back to fluid.
Muy fluido.
Very fluid understanding of reality.
One way to look at it: he's talking about form.
She's talking about form first.
So here's a form.
We have this thing we call a lectern.
Okay, that's a good start.
Is it really a lectern?
We have these different shapes and we call it a lectern.
Or is it oak?
But what is oak really?
It's wood.
So is it wood?
If we look really closely at the wood, is there really anything that's just really wood?
How could there be something called wood?
What's that made of?
There's cells in here.
Plant cells.
There's water in here.
There's sunlight in here.
If you look really, really close, there's atoms and molecules and some kind of array.
If you look really, really close, it's mostly actually space, right?
You may know a little bit about atomic theory, that the actual pieces of the atom are really fucking tiny.
It's like vast space, like here-to-the-moon amounts of space in between the neutrons and electrons and protons.
It's just a bunch of space.
Of course, it looks solid and it looks like it did last week, but we know that it's gradually decomposing and decaying and oxidating, and eventually it's just going to be dust, right?
So is it really a lectern?
That's one road into emptiness.
Another way to think about emptiness is holding everything that we perceive and think about in just such a radically light and open-handed way.
I'll try to write something about this and see what the problem with emptiness is.
The minute you write something down, it doesn't make any sense anymore.
I'll just redo what I wrote.
This made sense earlier.
Emptiness means no inherent existence.
No self-nature or own being.
Massively fluid.
And Avalokiteshvara, with the Buddha's blessing, says that each of the five Skandhas is empty, and provides this thorough formula: that form, all experience of physicality, is empty.
It's fluid and boundless.
We might think of things as solid and separate, but actually they're all changing and mixed together in a radical way.
Even the idea of emptiness is like this, not standing up on its own.
Radically interconnected.
There's no difference between the appearance of solidity to the form and also the total temporary and interpenetrated nature of all things.
If we grasp this thoroughly we lighten up.
We really lighten up in our attachments.
And we actually are not the least bit surprised anymore when things break down, get lost, vanish, are not what we thought they were.
And we're also not surprised when things appear and are invented and are right where we need them.
All things are a swirling vast experience of the empty nature of reality.
You can also say the radically interpenetrated nature of reality.
So then the sutra goes on.
This part starts to get very shorthand.
The rest of the sutra is very shorthand.

So he did the sutra, she did the sutra formula, Buddha, or whoever it is, about form: that form does not differ from emptiness, emptiness does not differ from form, form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself form.
And then when it says sensations, perceptions, formations, and consciousness are also like this, what that means is: sensations being vedana, and emptiness.
And emptiness does not differ from sensations.
Sensations themselves are emptiness.
And emptiness themselves are sensations.
And then you repeat the whole thing with perceptions, formations, and consciousness.
There are just many different ways to play with this and we'll try to explore it some more on Saturday.
Hopefully you'll be there.
And if you're not, maybe you can listen later to the talk on the website.
Because it's not just an idea.

It's really a felt and experienced kind of feeling for things that's very freeing, very liberating, where we don't have to hold on so tight or worry so much about things working out the way we think they're supposed to.
Because our idea of how they're supposed to work out, guess what that is?
Empty.
Having no inherent existence.
No real reality.
It's not total garbage.
It's based on something.
It has factors in it that made some kind of sense.
But the minute they come together, many other mysterious factors are there too that we can't even see, right?
And it's beyond our idea of what's supposed to happen.
Maybe that helps to explain the experience we all have, but we never seem to quite believe in this: the way that we have experiences where things completely go sideways, right?
Do not work out at all the way we wanted.
We're really upset and really bummed out because it's horrible.
And then sometimes later, sometimes not that long later, we realize, wow, that's exactly what needed to happen.
Perfect.
So that's an expression of emptiness, that way that things just are exactly the way they are, and work out.
Including suffering.
So that's my little dip into the waters of emptiness with you tonight.
Thank you.
I'm sorry there's not time for questions.
Maybe on Saturday we can do some discussion too.
Thanks.
